summary: This RFC discusses congestion in a packet switch with infinite storage. Such a switch never runs out of buffers, yet it can still become congested, since delay grows. It asks for discussion of the problem and solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 970 asks what congestion really is. It assumes a packet switch with unlimited memory and shows that even then, a network under heavy load can drop every packet, because queued packets run out of time before they are sent. The memo then proposes giving each sending host its own queue, so that every host gets an equal share of the link.

questions: what happens with infinite buffers in packet switches
why does congestion happen even with unlimited storage
why do queues cause packet loss
subtitle: Why a switch with unlimited memory can still lose every packet, and how per-host queues fix it.

tldr.problem: Earlier work treated congestion as the risk of a switch running out of buffer space. RFC 970 sets that aside and asks what congestion means when a switch has unlimited memory, and shows that the network can still fail completely.
tldr.mechanism: Under overload, packets wait so long in the queue that their time-to-live reaches zero and they are discarded at the next switch, so every packet is dropped. The memo proposes fair queuing: one queue per sending host, served in round-robin order, with Source Quench messages to tell a host when its own queue has grown too long.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a discussion document and says so: nothing in it is intended as a standard, and the hope is that a general consensus will emerge. It reports reproducing the packet-dropping effect on the author's own network and presents fair queuing as a direction for further work.

today: RFC 970 is a discussion memo, not a specification, and it says so in its status note: no solution proposed in it is intended as a standard for the ARPA-Internet, and the hope is that a general consensus will emerge. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC Editor lists its status as unknown.

sections.title: Congestion Without a Buffer Limit
sections.content:
Packet switching began when computer memory was several orders of magnitude more expensive than it is today, so engineers built switches with the absolute minimum of storage and treated congestion control as the business of avoiding buffer exhaustion. RFC 970 takes a different view. It starts by assuming infinite memory, which removes the questions of when to block and which packets to discard, and forces the harder question of how the system should behave.

The point of the assumption is to separate two problems that earlier work had treated as one. The memo argues that the order in which packets are transmitted is a design question in its own right, and that solving it for the infinite-storage case gives results that also apply to switches with finite memory.

Datagram systems are especially exposed, the memo notes, because they have no blocking mechanism of the kind a virtual circuit system provides. No fully effective solution to congestion in pure datagram systems is known, and most existing datagram systems behave badly under overload.
sections.plainLanguage: Early engineers built packet switches with as little memory as possible and treated congestion as the danger of running out of it. This RFC assumes unlimited memory instead, so it can ask a different question: in what order should a switch send the packets it is holding?

sections.title: How an Overloaded Switch Drops Every Packet
sections.content:
Each packet in the DoD Internet Protocol carries a time-to-live field, the number of seconds left before the packet must be discarded as uninteresting. The field is decremented as the packet travels, and a packet whose value reaches zero is dropped. The initial value is fixed, and in the DoD IP protocol it is 15 by default.

Consider a switch with one incoming link and one outgoing link where packets arrive faster than they leave. The queue on the outgoing link grows until the time a packet spends waiting exceeds its remaining lifetime. The switch then finds packets whose time-to-live has been decremented to zero and discards them, sending the packets that still have time. Once the steady state under overload is reached, every packet that leaves has a time-to-live of exactly one, because more than one packet is sent per time-to-live unit.

At the next switch, that value of one is decremented to zero and the packet is discarded. A datagram network with infinite storage, first-in-first-out queuing, at least two switches and a finite packet lifetime therefore drops all packets under overload. The memo reports seeing the effect experimentally: a load applied over a TCP connection produced a peak queue of 916 IP datagrams, although the connection timed out from the long round trip time before the predicted stable state was reached.

The result is not an artifact of infinite buffers, and the same thing happens with finite memory, where the effect is simply harder to see. The memo adds that the memory needed to avoid dropping a packet from buffer exhaustion is modest: for a switch with four 56Kb links and an upper bound on the time-to-live of 15 seconds, the maximum buffer space is 420K bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IP packet has a time-to-live counter that is reduced at each switch, and the packet is dropped when the counter reaches zero. When a queue grows longer than that lifetime, the switch can only send out packets with one second left, and the next switch throws them all away. Under heavy load, a network with unlimited memory can therefore deliver nothing at all.

sections.title: Fair Queuing: One Queue per Sending Host
sections.content:
The proposed fix is to stop treating every packet on an outgoing link as one queue. Each switch keeps a separate queue for each source host in the network and serves those queues in round-robin order, taking one packet from each non-empty queue in turn. Packets with a positive time-to-live are transmitted on the outgoing link, expired packets are dropped, and empty queues are skipped over and lose their turn.

Each source host then receives an equal share of the outgoing link, so a host that sends more packets does not get more bandwidth. The best strategy for a host becomes to send at the rate that keeps exactly one packet waiting in each switch, which gives that host its turn on every round-robin cycle and the minimum transit delay. The memo notes that this is acceptable from the network's point of view, since each queue will generally be between one and two packets long.

Hosts need advice from the network to find that rate. The memo reuses the existing Source Quench mechanism in DoD IP: a switch should send a Source Quench message to a source host whenever the number of packets in that host's queue exceeds a small value, probably two. A host that keeps its traffic just below the point at which Source Quench messages arrive keeps mean queue lengths below two for itself.

The memo is careful about the limits of the scheme. Making the switches fair does not make the network as a whole fair, so the approach suits a switch at a choke point, such as the entry node of a wide area network or an internetwork gateway, better than an intermediate node carrying packets from many hosts at different locations. The author does not claim it is a complete solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Give each sending host its own queue and take one packet from each queue in turn. Every host then gets the same share of the link, so sending more packets only makes that host's own traffic wait longer. Source Quench messages tell a host when its queue has grown past a small threshold.

sections.title: Why Self-Interest Breaks the Network
sections.content:
Each host can normally obtain more network bandwidth by transmitting more packets per unit of time, because first-in-first-out queuing gives the most resources to the sender of the most packets. Collectively, as hosts overload the network, total throughput drops, and as shown earlier it may drop to zero. The optimal strategy for each host is therefore strongly suboptimal for the network as a whole.

The memo compares this to the tragedy of the commons in economics, where each individual can improve their own position by using more of a free resource while the total amount of the resource degrades as the number of users increases, and notes the close analogy with the prisoner's dilemma. It groups the possible answers into three classes. Cooperative solutions, where everyone agrees to behave well, work for small numbers of players but break down as the number grows. Authoritarian solutions work when behaviour is easy to monitor, and fail when good behaviour is subtly defined. A market solution is possible only where the rules of the game can be changed so that the optimal strategy for one player is also optimal for all.

Fair queuing is the market-style answer, because the rules change so that sending more packets buys no extra bandwidth. The memo also records the limit of the approach: a malicious host, unlike a merely badly behaved one, can overload the network by sending from many different source addresses and impersonating a large number of hosts, thereby obtaining a larger share of the bandwidth. The memo calls that a network security problem and does not discuss it further.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host on its own gains by sending more packets, but together the hosts can drive total throughput down to zero. The memo compares this with a shared resource that everyone can over-use. It asks for the rules to change so that behaving well is also the best choice for one host, and fair queuing is how that is done.

sections.title: Implementing the Per-Host Queues
sections.content:
Keeping a separate queue for each source host on each outgoing link seems at first to add a lot of complexity to a switch. The memo argues that the manipulations are simpler than those required by, for example, a balanced binary tree. One simple implementation provides space for pointers in the header of each datagram buffer. The queue for each source host need only be singly linked, and the queue heads, which are the first buffer of each queue, need to be doubly linked so that a whole queue can be deleted when it becomes empty. That means three pointers in each buffer. More elaborate strategies can be devised to speed the process up when the queues are long, but the additional complexity is probably not justified in practice.

If buffer space does run out, the memo says to drop the packet at the end of the longest queue, since that is the packet that would be transmitted last. This is unfavourable to the host with the most datagrams in the network, which is in keeping with the goal of fairness.
sections.plainLanguage: One queue per host needs three pointers in each buffer and a list of queue heads that can be removed when empty. If buffers still fill up, the packet at the end of the longest queue is dropped, so the host sending the most packets is the one that loses the most.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO ANSWER THE OVERLOAD PROBLEM

items.title: Cooperative
items.text: Everyone agrees to behave well. Works for small numbers of hosts, breaks down as they grow.

items.title: Authoritarian
items.text: Behaviour is monitored and controlled. Fails when good behaviour is hard to define.

items.title: Market
items.text: The rules change so that the best choice for one host is also best for all.
